  "text": "In the spring the harbour office needed a new roof. Men came from inland and worked with a radio playing. For three days the village heard songs it did not know above the gulls.

Maren carried the tide books home in a box. Beneath them she found a photograph of her mother standing beside a bicycle. Agnes was young. One trouser leg was rolled to the knee, and her mouth was open at something outside the picture.

Maren put it on the kitchen shelf.

That evening Erris came to borrow a ruler. She had been given a map to draw for school.

"Was that your mother?"

"Yes."

"Where was she going?"

Maren took the photograph down. Behind the bicycle was a wall she did not recognise. There were leaves on a tree, broad leaves, nothing like the bent scrub above Skerrin.

"I don't know."

Erris accepted the ruler and promised to bring it back.

After she had gone, Maren turned the photograph over. There was no date. A little paper had come away at one corner where it had once been pasted somewhere.

She had time before she needed to leave. She made tea and sat with it, looking at the young woman and her bicycle. For forty years her mother had climbed the stair. Before that, there had been this afternoon.

At last Maren washed her cup. She put the photograph back on the shelf, facing the room.

Outside, the roofers had covered their work against the weather. The harbour smelled of cut timber. She took the longer road uphill."

  "text": "The longer road passed the old quarry, where rain lay in the wheel marks. Maren had not come this way since winter. Someone had cut back the brambles, exposing a gate she remembered as a child.

It stood open onto grass.

At the lighthouse she wound the clock and checked the western window. A little water had entered beneath the frame. She dried it with the cloth she kept behind the log, then sat down to enter the time.

From here the new roof of the harbour office was hidden. She could see only the road by which the men had arrived, pale between the houses, turning inland.

For a moment she tried to remember whether her mother had owned a bicycle. There had been a pump in the scullery, its hose bound with red thread. As a girl Maren had used it to blow dust from a crack in the floor. Nobody had told her to stop.

She wrote: Water at western window. Frame to be examined.

Then she closed the book.

The next afternoon Erris returned the ruler with her finished map. She had drawn the harbour larger than it was and run out of paper before reaching the quarry.

"I'll need another sheet," she said.

Maren found one in the desk. They laid the two sheets together on the kitchen table, holding the edges with cups.

Beyond the window a lorry reversed towards the harbour office. Its warning sounded three times, then ceased.

Erris bent over the join. Maren kept her hand on the paper while the road went across."

  "text": "By November the paste at the join had yellowed. Erris had left the map with Maren because there was nowhere at home to lay it flat. Sometimes, passing the kitchen table, Maren moved a cup from the harbour mouth or brushed crumbs from the inland road.

The quarry gate was on the second sheet. Beyond it Erris had drawn nothing.

Maren had meant to ask her about this, but when the girl came she was full of a dog that had followed her from school, and afterward the omission seemed too small to mention.

A carpenter repaired the western window. He showed Maren the rotten piece of sill, pressing his thumb into it as though she might otherwise doubt the work. Under the soft wood was a narrow channel packed with wings. Neither of them could say what insects they had been.

She entered the repair in the log. There was no further water.

One evening she stayed until the clock struck six. The harbour office had closed; its new roof held a pale remainder of daylight. She could make out someone walking the longer road, stopping now and then beside the hedge. At that distance she could not tell whether the person was coming towards the village or leaving it.

At home, she found the map had slipped partly off the table. She lifted it carefully, supporting the join.

Beneath it lay the ruler Erris had returned. Along one edge, where the girl had pressed too hard, a little blue ink remained.

Maren put it in the drawer, then took it out again."
